final_answer:
Short answer: No on both. On these facts the Lease is almost certainly a 'finance lease' under Virginia's UCC Article 2A (Va. Code Title 8.2A), and once Client accepted the Trailers its rent promises became irrevocable and independent of Lessor's and Manufacturer's performance. Client cannot lawfully withhold rent because of the compressor failures or Manufacturer's bankruptcy, and Lessor is not responsible for the defects. Client's recourse for the defects runs to Manufacturer (now a Chapter 7 debtor).

1. Finance lease. Under Va. Code 8.2A-103(1)(g) (uniform UCC 2A-103(1)(g)), a finance lease exists where (i) the lessor does not select, manufacture or supply the goods; (ii) the lessor acquires the goods in connection with the lease; and (iii) one of four conditions is met, including that the lessee receives a copy of the supply (purchase) contract before signing the lease, or receives the supplier's promises/warranties. Client picked the model and negotiated specs with Manufacturer; Lessor merely bought and financed; Lessor delivered a complete copy of the Manufacturer purchase agreement (with the two-year warranty) before Client signed. That satisfies the definition. Client is a business, so the consumer-lease exception does not apply. (Caveat: I could not retrieve the Virginia statutory text directly; I rely on the uniform text as reflected in secondary sources and the uniform version adopted in Virginia, and recommend confirming the Virginia text.)

2. Hell-or-high-water. Under 8.2A-407, in a finance lease that is not a consumer lease, the lessee's promises become irrevocable and independent upon acceptance of the goods; the promise is enforceable by the lessor and its assignees and is not subject to cancellation, termination, modification, repudiation, excuse or substitution without the consent of the party to whom it runs. The section is self-executing, and in any event the Lease's express 'absolute and unconditional, irrespective of any defense or setoff, counterclaim, or recoupment' language says the same thing. Client used the Trailers for four months, so acceptance (8.2A-515) is very likely. The defects arose after acceptance and are not an excuse to stop paying; Client's stopping payment is a lessee default exposing it to Lessor's remedies (8.2A-523 et seq.: accelerated rent/damages, repossession, plus any lease-specified costs and fees).

3. Lessor not liable for the defects. Lessor made no warranties; in a finance lease the lessor gives no implied warranty of merchantability or fitness (8.2A-212, 8.2A-213 exclude finance lessors), and express warranties arise only from the lessor's own statements (8.2A-210). Instead, 8.2A-209 extends the supplier's promises and warranties (including Manufacturer's two-year warranty) to Client as lessee, subject to the warranty's terms and the supplier's defenses, and Client's remedies lie against Manufacturer. The Lease's direction to pursue equipment claims against Manufacturer is consistent with this. Manufacturer's Chapter 7 and the trustee's refusal to honor the warranty do not shift the risk to Lessor; the statutory risk allocation puts supplier-insolvency risk on the lessee. Client should file a (likely unsecured, largely uncollectible) proof of claim in the Chapter 7 case, check for warranty insurance, extended-warranty or component-maker (compressor/refrigeration unit OEM) warranties, and check whether Manufacturer's refrigeration unit supplier will honor a direct warranty.

4. Limits and counterarguments (none on these facts appears to change the bottom line). The hell-or-high-water rule does not protect a lessor from fraud, from failure to give a reasonable opportunity to inspect/reject before acceptance, or from unconscionability or good-faith limits (8.2A-108, 1-304). Nothing in the facts suggests Lessor fraud, misrepresentation, or that Lessor selected or supplied the goods. Revocation of acceptance against a finance lessor is narrowly limited (8.2A-517) and four months of use with a promised repair undermines any such claim; the lessee's right to revoke generally runs against the supplier. Lessee may still sue for damages for a lessor's own breach (8.2A-407 does not bar that) but not withhold rent. A recharacterization argument (that Lessor is really a seller/financer who 'supplied' the goods or participated in selection) is not supported here. If Lessor assigned the Lease, the assignee takes free of the lessee's defenses as well.

Practical advice: cure the default and resume payment (or negotiate a forbearance/payment modification, substitute equipment, or a buy-out) to avoid acceleration and repossession; pursue Manufacturer's estate and any third-party warranty or insurer for repair cost; keep records of repair costs and downtime for the proof of claim. Confidence: high on the bottom line, moderate on precise Virginia section wording because primary Virginia text and any Virginia case law could not be retrieved within the tool limits; I identified no Virginia case in this run.
